study.title: Somatosensory Stimulation With XNKQ Acupuncture Modulates Functional Connectivity of Motor Areas
study.study_design: 2 × 2 factorial within-subject design, four different interventions in four different sessions (four different days with at least 24 h in between each) in a random order
study.randomization: Random order of interventions across sessions
study.blinding: Subjects were blinded regarding the point specificity (acupuncture points vs. non-acupuncture points). Only the subjects were blinded for the applied acupuncture conditions as well as the researchers analyzing the data during the first stages of analyses. The acupuncturist applying the manual acupuncture could not be blinded for the different conditions.
study.population: Healthy volunteers between 18 and 36 years of age
study.inclusion_criteria: Healthy volunteers between 18 and 36 years of age; all right-handed [laterality score: 90.1 ± 17.3 (SD)]; underwent a clinical neurological examination; confirmed they were not taking any medications for acute or chronic diseases
study.exclusion_criteria: Taking medications for acute or chronic diseases; not right-handed (implied by Edinburgh inventory criterion)

interventions.procedure_label_exact: XNKQ acupuncture as manual needle-stimulation on five acupuncture points (DU26 unilaterally, PC6 and SP6 bilaterally)
interventions.anatomical_location_exact: PC6: 2 cun above the transverse crease of the wrist, between the tendons of radial wrist flexor and palmaris longus; DU26: at the junction of the upper 1/3 and middle 1/3 of the philtrum; SP6: 3 cun above the tip of the medial malleolus, behind the posterior border of the medial aspect of the tibia
interventions.laterality_exact: PC6 bilateral, DU26 unilateral, SP6 bilateral
interventions.needle_type_exact: sterile, single use, individually wrapped acupuncture needles; titanium, DongBang, Acupuncture, Inc., Boryeong, Korea
interventions.depth_exact: PC6: 0.5–1.0 cun; DU26: ∼0.3–0.5 cun obliquely toward the nasal septum; SP6: ∼0.5–1.0 cun obliquely along with the medial border of the tibia
interventions.manipulation_exact: PC6: reducing method by lifting and thrusting with simultaneous twirling manipulation for 1 min (twirling anticlockwise with the left hand and clockwise with the right hand); DU26: bird-pecking needling until the eyes became wet or developed tears; SP6: lifting and thrusting reinforcing manipulation, thrusts with heavy strength and lifting with gentle strength for 1 min
interventions.deqi_intended_exact: deqi intended; DU26 stimulated until the eyes became wet or developed tears
interventions.needle_retention_exact: needles were removed directly after stimulation [called 'quick needles' technique]
interventions.number_of_sessions_exact: 1 session per day, 4 sessions total across 4 days
interventions.treatment_period_exact: four different days with at least 24 h in between each
interventions.practitioner_description_exact: acupuncturist from Tianjin University of Traditional Chinese Medicine (YC) trained for 12 years and with 8 years of clinical experience; trained directly by the developer of the XNKQ acupuncture
interventions.participant_instructions_exact: subjects were informed that they would receive acupuncture with five needles at the lower leg, the forearm, and above the upper lip on four separate days, on 2 days with stimulation of the needle and on the other two without
interventions.treatment_rationale_given_exact: Xingnao Kaiqiao (XNKQ) acupuncture is a semi-standardized manual acupuncture technique developed in Tianjin, China, by Professor Shi Xuemin using a specific set of acupuncture points and strong needle-stimulation for different neuropathological conditions such as acute and chronic stroke symptoms

neuroimaging_methods.smoothing_exact: 6 mm FWHM smoothing performed on the individual ECM maps (after Z-standard transformation); no spatial smoothing before the centrality analysis
neuroimaging_methods.motion_exclusion_exact: frame-wise displacement (FD) calculated using BRAMILA tools; average FD 0.14 ± 0.06 mm; average percentage of volumes exceeding an FD-threshold of 0.5 mm was 1.9 ± 2.8%; no subjects excluded based on motion (no significant difference in head motion across scans, all p > 0.46)
neuroimaging_methods.filtering_exact: temporal band-pass filtering (0.01–0.08 Hz) using REST toolbox
neuroimaging_methods.global_signal_regression_exact: global mean signal was NOT regressed out

extraction_notes.note: The paper reports T-values for individual peaks within a single significant cluster for the XNKQ vs. npws ECM contrast, but does not provide cluster-level statistics (cluster size in voxels, cluster-level p-value). All peaks appear to belong to one cluster described as 'mainly subcortical' but this is not entirely clear from the text.
For the stimulation main effect ECM result, two peaks are reported (precuneus and cuneus) but it is unclear whether these are two separate clusters or peaks within the same cluster.
No adverse events section is present in the paper. It is not reported whether adverse events were monitored or occurred.
No expectancy or credibility measures beyond MASS needle sensation were reported. The paper does not state that expectancy was formally assessed.

The seed-based analysis is described as post-hoc and without formal statistics ('no formal statistics was applied in this step (double dipping)'). The coordinates and T-values from this analysis are used for visualization only. This should be considered when interpreting these results.
Needle retention time is stated as 'removed directly after stimulation' for XNKQ (quick needles technique). For control conditions (no stimulation), retention time is not explicitly reported.
The exact number of volumes per resting-state scan is not reported (only that the first 10 volumes were removed). Total scan duration for each resting-state run is not specified.

The 2×2 within-subject design means all 24 subjects contributed data to all four arms. The arms are not independent groups but repeated measurements within individuals. This is preserved in the extraction but should be noted for meta-analytic purposes.

For the XNKQ vs. npns and XNKQ vs. pns ECM comparisons, the paper states 'No significant effect was found.' It is unclear whether these were planned contrasts in the factorial model or post-hoc pairwise comparisons.

The paper states that the precuneus result for the stimulation main effect 'was driven by the stimulation of non-acupuncture points (non-points with stimulation, npws)' — specifically that it 'was significant for npws vs. pns and npws vs. npns, and was not significant when XNKQ was compared to pns and XNKQ vs. npns.' However, the XNKQ vs. npws comparison also showed no significant difference in precuneus. This pattern of results is somewhat complex and the exact post-hoc tests used to derive these statements are not fully specified.

Clinical outcomes beyond needle sensation (MASS) are not reported. The study focuses on neuroimaging outcomes. No pain scales, stroke-specific outcomes, or motor function assessments are administered since the sample is healthy volunteers.
The paper describes the MASS as measuring 'needle sensation as a proxy for deqi and pain sensation' but does not report individual MASS subscale scores — only the aggregate MASS index per condition.
